blocks.text: 1. Metadata Extraction

blocks.alt: A document goes through metadata extraction to produce structured metadata

blocks.text: Metadata Extraction covers how structured information gets pulled from normalized text, shifting focus from the text itself to information about that text.
It captures information about a document beyond its raw text content, a structured layer that sits alongside the text itself.
2. Content Versus Metadata

blocks.alt: Content is the text itself while metadata is data about the text

blocks.text: A document's content is what it says; metadata is information about the document itself.
These are two distinct kinds of information.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Kind of information","Example"],"rows":[["Content","The actual sentences and paragraphs of the document"],["Metadata","Author, source, creation date, title"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Common Metadata Fields

blocks.alt: Author, date, and source are example metadata fields

blocks.text: Author, source, creation date, and title are all common metadata fields.
Each field captures something the raw text alone does not state.
4. Extracting From File Structure
Some metadata already lives in the file itself, like a PDF's embedded author field.
This is related to how PDF Parsing preserves tables and layout, another form of structural extraction.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A PDF often carries a title, author, and creation date directly in its file properties, meaning that metadata can sometimes be read without any inference at all.

blocks.text: 5. Inferring Metadata From Content

blocks.alt: Document content produces an inferred topic or category

blocks.text: When explicit metadata is missing, it can sometimes be inferred from the text itself.
A heading or opening sentence often reveals a topic or category.
6. Why Metadata Improves Retrieval

blocks.alt: A query filters by metadata to produce narrowed results

blocks.text: Metadata lets a retrieval system filter results before or after semantic search.
What Is RAG covers retrieval using embeddings; metadata adds a second, complementary filtering signal on top of that.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Filtering by metadata lets a system narrow a search to only recent documents, or only a specific author, before semantic similarity ever gets computed, often making retrieval both faster and more precise.

blocks.text: 7. Attaching Metadata To Chunks
Once a document is later split into chunks, each chunk needs to inherit its parent document's metadata.
Without that inheritance, a retrieved chunk loses its surrounding context entirely.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Without inherited metadata","With inherited metadata"],"rows":[["A retrieved chunk is just isolated text","A retrieved chunk still knows its source, author, and date"],["Filtering by source is impossible after chunking","Filtering by source still works after chunking"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Metadata As The Bridge To Structure
Metadata bridges raw, unstructured text back to the structured information a system can filter on.
This completes the preparation steps that come before deduplication, covered next.
9. Recognizing When Metadata Extraction Deserves Extra Investment

blocks.alt: Needing filtered or attributed retrieval points toward investing in metadata extraction

blocks.text: Large, multi-source document collections benefit most from rich metadata.
Small, single-source collections need only minimal metadata.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Discarding available file metadata like author and creation date without extracting it.
Never inferring basic metadata like a title when explicit fields are missing.
Forgetting that chunks need to inherit their parent document's metadata after splitting.
Treating metadata as optional decoration rather than a genuine filtering signal for retrieval.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Metadata extraction captures information about a document beyond its raw text content.
Content is what a document says; metadata is information about the document itself.
Common metadata fields include author, source, creation date, and title.
Some metadata already lives in the file itself, like a PDF's embedded properties.
When explicit metadata is missing, it can sometimes be inferred from the text.
Metadata lets a retrieval system filter results as a complementary signal to semantic search.
Each chunk produced later needs to inherit its parent document's metadata.
Metadata bridges unstructured text back to structured, filterable information.
